::: {.resource-intro}
**The essential idea:** Synthesis compares evidence across sources to explain patterns, disagreements, limitations, and open questions. It is more than a sequence of article summaries.
:::

## Core practices

### Build a comparison matrix

Track questions, methods, settings, findings, limitations, and relevance in consistent columns.

### Look across rows

Group studies by their shared claim, divergent result, method, scale, or context.

### Write from a claim

Begin a paragraph with a supported cross-study observation, then use individual studies as evidence and explain any important differences.

## A simple workflow

Choose three related studies. Complete a matrix with comparable fields. Identify one agreement and one apparent disagreement, then investigate whether design, site, population, or measurement explains the difference.

## In context

::: {.callout-example}
Three urban heat studies may report different magnitudes of cooling from tree cover. A synthesis asks which outcomes were measured and in which climates before concluding that the findings conflict.
:::

## Keep in mind

Do not treat a small number of studies as field-wide consensus. Distinguish evidence, interpretation, and uncertainty.
